Why this theme matters

This theme page collects 10 English passages that touch humility as a philosophical concern—whether as a concept to define, a value to pursue, or a problem to examine.

In the history of philosophy

Related discussions appear across Greek, Chinese, Indian, Islamic, and modern European traditions. Use the quotations below as entry points, then follow thinker pages for fuller context.

Frequently asked questions

What did philosophers say about humility?

They approached humility from ethics, metaphysics, politics, and lived practice. The passages below show several of those angles in compact form.

Where can I find philosophy quotes about humility?

This archive page is organized for that search intent: verified English quotations, with links to thinkers and related themes.

How should I read these quotations?

Read the sentence first, then check school and source. A quotation is a doorway into an argument, not a substitute for the surrounding text.

  1. What I do not know, I do not claim to know.
    Socrates
    Socratic School
  2. The beginning of philosophy is a consciousness of one's own weakness and inability concerning necessary things.
    Epictetus
    Stoicism
  3. What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know.
    Augustine of Hippo
    Patristic Philosophy
  4. What do I know?
    Michel de Montaigne
    Renaissance Humanism
  5. Any man can err; only a fool persists in error.
    Cicero
    Roman Philosophy
  6. The Master said: You, shall I teach you what knowing is? To know what you know, and to know what you do not know — that is true knowing.
    Confucius
    Confucianism
  7. The Master said: When three people walk together, one of them is sure to be my teacher. I select what is good in them and follow it; what is not good, I correct in myself.
    Confucius
    Confucianism
  8. Teach your tongue to say, “I do not know.”
    Talmudic tradition
    Rabbinic Judaism
  9. Our knowledge can only be finite, while our ignorance must necessarily be infinite.
    Karl Popper
    Critical Rationalism
  10. It is of great use to the sailor to know the length of his line, though he cannot with it fathom all the depths of the ocean.
    John Locke
    British Empiricism
